p: Which statement describes the config and state containers used throughout OpenConfig models?
o: config is used over NETCONF, and state is used over RESTCONF, so each protocol reads a different container
config and state are alternatives in a YANG choice, so each node holds either configuration or operational data, never both at once
config holds the running configuration, and state holds the startup configuration saved on the device
config holds the intended values a client sets, and state repeats those leaves as applied values plus operational counters
e: OpenConfig separates intended configuration (config, read-write) from what the device has applied and reports (state, read-only). Comparing the two shows whether a change has taken effect.

p: Match each part of a NETCONF exchange with the protocol layer it belongs to.
e: RFC 6241 layers NETCONF as secure transport, messages (rpc, rpc-reply, notification), operations (get-config, edit-config and so on), and content, which YANG models define.
s: Configuration data structured by YANG models

p: ietf-ip augments ietf-interfaces. Which body for PUT /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback20 sets 10.20.0.1/32?
o: {"ietf-interfaces:interface": [{"name": "Loopback20", "type": "iana-if-type:softwareLoopback", "ietf-ip:ipv4": {"address": {"ip": "10.20.0.1", "prefix-length": 32}}}]}
{"ietf-interfaces:interface": [{"name": "Loopback20", "type": "iana-if-type:softwareLoopback", "ietf-ip:ipv4": {"address": [{"ip": "10.20.0.1", "prefix-length": 32}]}}]}
{"ietf-interfaces:interface": [{"name": "Loopback20", "type": "iana-if-type:softwareLoopback", "ietf-ip:ipv4": {"address": [{"ip": "10.20.0.1", "ip:prefix-length": 32}]}}]}
{"ietf-interfaces:interface": [{"name": "Loopback20", "type": "iana-if-type:softwareLoopback", "ipv4": {"address": [{"ip": "10.20.0.1", "prefix-length": 32}]}}]}
e: ipv4 comes from a different module than interface, so it's prefixed with the module name, ietf-ip. Its children share its module and stay unprefixed. address is a list, so it's an array, and tree prefixes such as ip: never appear in JSON.
c:
module: ietf-interfaces
  +--rw interfaces
     +--rw interface* [name]
        +--rw name                 string
        +--rw type                 identityref
        +--rw ip:ipv4!
           +--rw ip:enabled?   boolean
           +--rw ip:address* [ip]
              +--rw ip:ip                 inet:ipv4-address-no-zone
              +--rw (ip:subnet)
                 +--:(ip:prefix-length)
                    +--rw ip:prefix-length?   uint8

p: Which pyang output format gives an XML instance skeleton of a module that you can fill in to build an edit-config payload?
o: -f jstree
-f yin, which writes the module out as XML so it can be edited into an instance payload
-f tree
-f sample-xml-skeleton
e: sample-xml-skeleton prints empty instance XML in the module's namespace. yin is the YANG module itself written as XML, which is a schema, not data. tree and jstree only show structure.

p: What does the x at the start of the interfaces-state lines mean?
o: Those nodes are RPCs, which are invoked with POST
Those nodes aren't supported on this particular device, as declared in a deviation module that the device publishes
Those nodes are actions, which run on a single list entry
Those nodes have status deprecated, so new code should read state from interfaces instead
e: The first character of each line is the status: + current, x deprecated, o obsolete. RPCs and actions show -x after the status, as +---x. ietf-interfaces moved state into interfaces when it adopted NMDA.
c:
module: ietf-interfaces
  +--rw interfaces
  |  +--rw interface* [name]
  |     +--rw name            string
  |     +--ro oper-status     enumeration
  x--ro interfaces-state
     x--ro interface* [name]
        x--ro name            string
        x--ro oper-status     enumeration

p: Which two statements about this tree are true? (Choose two.)
o: import-rt can hold several string values for each VRF
import-rt is a list, so each of its entries needs its own key leaf
route-count can be read, for example with content=nonconfig, but never set
rd is mandatory, because a VRF can't work without a route distinguisher
route-count can be set to 0 to clear a VRF's routing table
e: * without brackets marks a leaf-list of values, and ro marks state data that can't be configured. rd has ? and is optional in this model, whatever the protocol needs.
c:
module: example-vrf
  +--rw vrfs
     +--rw vrf* [name]
        +--rw name           string
        +--rw rd?            string
        +--rw import-rt*     string
        +--ro route-count?   uint32
        +--rw description?   string

p: A script must manage a mixed fleet whose platforms aren't recorded anywhere. How can Netmiko pick the right device_type?
o: Leave device_type out, and Netmiko reads the platform from the SSH banner
Set device_type="autodetect" in ConnectHandler, which then picks the platform itself for each command
Set device_type="generic", which works the same way as the platform drivers
Use SSHDetect(**dev).autodetect() and pass the result as device_type
e: SSHDetect connects with the autodetect type, runs probe commands and returns the best match, such as cisco_xe. ConnectHandler needs a concrete type, and generic lacks the platform's prompt and paging handling.

p: The switches are only reachable through a bastion host. How can Netmiko reach them?
o: Set fast_cli=False, which lets Netmiko forward the session through the bastion
Pass the bastion's address as host and the switch's address as secret
Run send_command("ssh switch") on a session to the bastion, which Netmiko does for every device type
Pass ssh_config_file pointing to an SSH config that sets ProxyJump or ProxyCommand for those hosts
e: Netmiko can read an OpenSSH config file, so a proxy defined there is used for the connection. Driving a second SSH from the bastion's shell works poorly, because the prompts and device type no longer match.

p: A monitoring script must receive NETCONF event notifications as they occur. Which ncclient calls fit?
o: m.edit_config() with a notification element, then m.get_config()
m.get() in a loop every second, comparing each reply with the last
m.create_subscription(), then m.take_notification() in a loop
m.dispatch("listen"), then m.close_session() to flush events
e: create-subscription (RFC 5277) starts an event stream on the session, and take_notification blocks until the next notification arrives. Polling with get isn't event-driven.

p: What does device_params={"name": "iosxe"} do in this call?
o: It selects Cisco-IOS-XE-native as the default model for every RPC sent on this session, so payloads need no namespace
It tells the device to start its NETCONF agent if it isn't running
It loads ncclient's IOS XE device handler, for vendor-specific capabilities and behavior
It sets the session to exchange JSON instead of XML with the device
e: Device handlers adjust ncclient for a platform, for example extra capabilities or RPCs. The protocol stays XML over SSH, and models are chosen by the namespaces in each payload.
c:
m = manager.connect(host="10.0.0.11", port=830,
                    username=user, password=pw,
                    hostkey_verify=False,
                    device_params={"name": "iosxe"})

p: In the native model, static routes are a list keyed by prefix and mask. Which URL reads the route to 10.0.0.0/8?
o: /restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/ip/route/ip-route-interface-forwarding-list=10.0.0.0,255.0.0.0
/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/ip/route/ip-route-interface-forwarding-list?prefix=10.0.0.0&mask=255.0.0.0
/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/ip/route/ip-route-interface-forwarding-list=10.0.0.0%2F8
/restconf/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-native:native/ip/route/ip-route-interface-forwarding-list=10.0.0.0/255.0.0.0
e: RESTCONF separates multiple key values with commas, in the order the keys are defined. A slash would start a new path segment, and keys never go in the query string.

p: Which expression returns the five-minute CPU average?
o: r.json()["Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:cpu-utilization"]["five-minutes"]
r.json()["Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:cpu-utilization"]["Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:five-minutes"]
r.json()["Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:cpu-usage"]["cpu-utilization"]["five-minutes"]
r.json()["cpu-utilization"]["five-minutes"]
e: The reply's single member is the requested node, qualified with its module, not its parent. Children in the same module have no prefix.
c:
url = f"{base}/data/Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:cpu-usage/cpu-utilization"
r = requests.get(url, auth=auth, verify="corp-ca.pem",
                 headers={"Accept": "application/yang-data+json"})
# Reply begins: {"Cisco-IOS-XE-process-cpu-oper:cpu-utilization": {"five-seconds": 3, ...
cpu = ________

p: A pipeline makes Loopback30 exactly match a stored body, and it must be safe to rerun. Which method fits?
o: PUT to the interface's URL, which creates or replaces it the same way every time
POST to the interfaces list, which creates the interface on every run
DELETE followed by POST, which recreates the interface on every run
PATCH to the interface's URL, which merges the body and leaves any extra settings
e: PUT is idempotent and replaces the target, so repeated runs give the same state (201, then 204). POST fails on the second run, PATCH can leave drift behind, and delete-then-create causes an outage each time.

p: Which Ansible module pushes a YANG XML payload to IOS XE over NETCONF?
o: ansible.netcommon.netconf_config, with connection: ansible.netcommon.netconf
cisco.ios.ios_config, with src pointing to the XML file, which it converts into an edit-config RPC
ansible.builtin.uri, with the payload as the body
ansible.netcommon.netconf_get, with the payload as its filter
e: netconf_config sends edit-config with the given content over a NETCONF connection. ios_config is a CLI module, netconf_get only reads, and uri speaks HTTP.

p: What does this task do?
o: It deletes the VLANs that a previous run created
It deletes every VLAN configured on the switch, because no config list is given
It deletes only VLANs that no interface currently uses
It deletes nothing, because there's no config list naming which VLANs to delete
e: For resource modules, deleted with no config removes all configuration of that resource, except platform defaults such as VLAN 1. Listing VLANs limits the deletion to them.
c:
- name: Clean up VLANs
  cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
    state: deleted

p: A ZTP setup serves the script from a TFTP server rather than a URL. Which DHCP options must the pool provide?
o: Option 150 with the TFTP server's address, and option 43 with the script's file name
Option 43 with the TFTP server's address, and option 67 with the script's file name
Option 150 with the TFTP server's address, and option 67 with the script's file name
Option 67 alone, with the server and file name joined by a colon
e: Option 150 gives Cisco devices the TFTP server, and option 67 names the file. Option 43 is the vendor option that PnP uses, and option 67 alone needs a full URL.

p: A router boots with no configuration and gets a DHCP address with option 150, but no option 67. Which files does IOS AutoInstall request over TFTP?
o: A Python script named ztp.py, which it runs in Guest Shell
Nothing, because AutoInstall needs Catalyst Center or a DHCP bootfile option to tell it which file names to request
A network-wide file such as network-confg, then a host-specific file such as <hostname>-confg
The startup-config file of the TFTP server itself
e: Without a bootfile, AutoInstall tries default names: a network config to learn its hostname, then a host-specific config. ZTP's Python script is only used when option 67 names it.

p: HTTPS to the switch works, but every RESTCONF URL, including /restconf itself, returns 404. What's the most likely cause?
o: The URLs aren't percent-encoded, so the server can't find them
The user lacks privilege 15, so RESTCONF hides its resources
The restconf command isn't configured, so the HTTPS server has no RESTCONF resources
The Accept header asks for JSON, which this switch doesn't support
e: The web server answers, but nothing is registered under /restconf until restconf is enabled. Missing rights give 401 or 403, and an unsupported media type gives 406 or 415.

p: A NETCONF commit fails with this error. What's wrong?
o: A member value names an interface that doesn't exist, which the leafref doesn't allow
Another NETCONF session holds a lock on the candidate datastore, so the member values can't be saved yet
The member leaf-list is mandatory, and the payload left it empty
The lag entry already exists, so it can't be created again
e: instance-required is the error-app-tag for a leafref whose target doesn't exist. Create the interface first, or correct the name.

p: Match each EEM event detector with when it triggers the applet.
e: Each detector watches a different source. event none has no trigger of its own, so the applet runs only when invoked by name, which suits on-demand tools.
r: Only when run with event manager run
When a matching log message is generated

p: Why does action 2.0 include pattern "confirm"?
o: pattern runs the command in confirm mode, so action 3.0 is ignored
pattern makes the applet run only when the word confirm appears in the log
clear counters asks for confirmation, so EEM waits for that prompt instead of the router prompt, and action 3.0 answers it
pattern filters the command's output, so only lines containing the word confirm are kept in $_cli_result for action 3.0 to read
e: By default an EEM cli action waits for the exec prompt. pattern tells it to stop at a different prompt, so the next action can reply.
c:
event manager applet CLEAR-COUNTERS
 event timer cron cron-entry "0 0 * * 1"
 action 1.0 cli command "enable"
 action 2.0 cli command "clear counters" pattern "confirm"
 action 3.0 cli command "y"

p: Put the steps that let a Catalyst Center PnP claim apply a Day-0 template in order.
e: PnP templates live in Onboarding Configuration projects, and only committed versions can be used, so the claim comes last.
s: Claim the device to a site with the template and its variable values
Create a project in Onboarding Configuration
Create the template, with variables, inside that project

p: A new MX must use a static WAN address, because the site has no DHCP on the uplink. How can this be set before the MX arrives?
o: PUT /networks/{networkId}/appliance/uplinks/settings on the switch at the site
PUT /devices/{serial}/managementInterface with wan1 set to a static address, gateway and DNS
PUT /networks/{networkId}/appliance/vlans with the WAN address, gateway and DNS servers set on VLAN 1 for the uplink
POST /networks/{networkId}/devices/claim with the IP address in the body
e: The management interface settings for an MX's uplinks can be set on the serial ahead of time, so the device uses them when it boots. VLAN settings cover the LAN side.

p: In the Plug and Play Connect portal, what tells a new Catalyst SD-WAN edge which overlay to join?
o: The device template attached in SD-WAN Manager, which the portal copies to the device along with its certificate and serial
The device's serial number, which encodes the address of its Validator
A DHCP option 43 string configured inside the portal for the device
The controller profile assigned to the device, which holds the Validator's address and the organization name
e: PnP Connect redirects the device using its controller profile. The Validator then authenticates it, and the organization name must match the overlay's.

p: A Catalyst Center API returns executionId and executionStatusUrl instead of a taskId. What should the script do?
o: Wait for a webhook, because executions can't be polled
Treat the change as complete, because executionId is only returned on success
Poll the executionStatusUrl until its status is SUCCESS or FAILURE, then check bapiError if it failed
Treat executionId as a taskId, and poll /dna/intent/api/v1/task/{executionId} until isError and endTime appear
e: Business APIs return an execution, tracked at /dna/platform/management/business-api/v1/execution-status/{executionId}. Its status and error fields report the outcome.

p: A script calls GET /networks/{networkId}/devices for each of 300 networks to collect switch serials, and keeps hitting 429. What's the better design?
o: The same per-network calls, made with a second API key
One paginated GET /organizations/{organizationId}/devices with productTypes[]=switch
The same per-network calls, made in 20 parallel threads
GET /organizations/{organizationId}/inventory/devices once, with perPage set high enough to skip pagination
e: Organization-wide endpoints return everything in a few paged calls instead of hundreds. The rate limit is per organization, so threads and extra keys make it worse.

p: A script logs in to SD-WAN Manager every minute and never logs out. After some hours, new logins start failing. What's the fix?
o: Reuse one session, or call logout after each run so sessions don't pile up
Disable XSRF checking, which is what blocks the new logins
Log in twice each time, because the first login always times out
Send the password in a header on each request instead of logging in
e: SD-WAN Manager limits concurrent sessions per user, and abandoned sessions count until they expire. Reuse or close them.

p: A script needs the live session details for one endpoint MAC, such as the NAS IP, switch port and authorization result. Which ISE API fits?
o: The pxGrid ANC topic, read once for the MAC
The ERS network device API, filtered by the endpoint's MAC
The ERS endpoint API, which stores session details on each endpoint
The Monitoring (MnT) API session lookup by MAC address
e: MnT exposes active session data, such as /admin/API/mnt/Session/MACAddress/{mac}. ERS holds configuration objects, not live sessions, and pxGrid ANC covers quarantine actions.

p: What priorities does this render for the three VLANs?
e: loop.cycle steps through its arguments, one per iteration, and starts again at the first when it runs out.

p: What does this line render?
o: switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,10,20,20,30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 20,10,30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 30,20,10
e: map takes the ids, unique drops repeats, sort orders the numbers ascending, and join builds the string.
c:
{# ports = [{"id": 20}, {"id": 10}, {"id": 20}, {"id": 30}, {"id": 10}] #}
switchport trunk allowed vlan {{ ports | map(attribute="id") | unique | sort | join(",") }}

p: What does this render?
o: Both lines indented by two spaces, because indent adds to the template's space
Both lines indented by one space, because the template supplies the first line's space
Neither line indented, because indent needs first=True
Only the first line indented, because indent skips the lines after it
e: indent indents every line except the first by default (first=False). Here the template's own space covers the first line, so both lines end up one space in.

p: A cisco.meraki task fails with an error saying the meraki SDK can't be imported. What's the fix?
o: Add the API key to the inventory, which loads the SDK
Change the connection to network_cli, so the module talks to the Dashboard through the devices instead of the SDK
Install the meraki Python package in the interpreter Ansible uses on the control node
Install the meraki package on each Meraki device
e: The collection's modules run locally and call the Dashboard through the meraki SDK, so it must be installed in the control node's Python, the one ansible_python_interpreter points to for localhost.

p: What does delegate_to: localhost do in this play?
o: It runs the API call once in total, on the control node, for the first switch only
It runs the API call on the control node once for each switch, using that switch's variables
It runs the call on each switch, then copies each registered result back to localhost so later tasks can read it
It runs the API call on each switch, which then forwards it to Catalyst Center
e: Delegation changes where the task runs, not which host's variables it uses, so ansible_host and cc_dev belong to each switch in turn. run_once would limit it to one run.
c:
- hosts: switches
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: Look up each switch in Catalyst Center
      ansible.builtin.uri:
        url: "https://{{ cc_host }}/dna/intent/api/v1/network-device?managementIpAddress={{ ansible_host }}"
        headers: {X-Auth-Token: "{{ token }}"}
      delegate_to: localhost
      register: cc_dev

p: A playbook creates a Catalyst Center site with uri, but every rerun fails because the site already exists. What makes it idempotent?
o: Use PUT instead of POST, because PUT creates the site the first time and updates it, without error, on every rerun
GET the site by name first, register the result, and POST only when it isn't found
Add ignore_errors: true to the POST task, so reruns don't fail
Add retries: 3 to the POST task, so a later attempt succeeds
e: uri has no idea of desired state, so the playbook must check first. ignore_errors hides real failures too.

p: Which ERS request sets the SGACL that applies from source group Contractors to destination group Servers?
o: PUT /ers/config/sgt/{id} on the Contractors group, with the Servers group and the SGACL added to its definition
POST /ers/config/sgacl with the two groups' names in its description
POST /ers/config/ancpolicy with the source and destination groups
POST /ers/config/egressmatrixcell with sourceSgtId, destinationSgtId and the SGACL IDs
e: Each cell of the TrustSec egress matrix links a source SGT, a destination SGT and the SGACLs between them. An SGACL on its own isn't bound to any pair of groups.

p: Compliance requires every enabled SSID to use WPA2-Enterprise with an external RADIUS server. Which expression lists the SSIDs that break the rule?
o: [s["name"] for s in ssids if s["enabled"] and s["encryptionMode"] != "8021x-radius"]
[s["name"] for s in ssids if s["enabled"] and s["authMode"] == "psk"]
[s["name"] for s in ssids if s["enabled"] and s["authMode"] != "8021x-radius"]
[s["name"] for s in ssids if s["authMode"] != "8021x-radius"]
e: The API returns every SSID slot, including disabled ones, so filtering on enabled avoids false alarms. authMode holds the authentication type, and checking only for psk would miss open SSIDs.

p: Branches in a Catalyst SD-WAN service VPN must reach only the data center hubs, not each other. Which policy type does that?
o: A QoS policy that sets branch-to-branch traffic to the lowest priority
A localized ACL on each branch's LAN interface that denies the other branches' subnets
A centralized control policy that limits which routes and TLOCs are advertised to the branches
A centralized data policy on the branches that drops branch-to-branch traffic once it arrives over the overlay
e: Control policies shape the overlay's topology on the Controllers, so branches never learn each other's routes. Data policies and ACLs filter traffic after the paths already exist.

p: A Catalyst Center script works from a laptop but times out from a CI runner that has HTTPS_PROXY set. What's the likely fix?
o: Raise the request timeout to 300 seconds
Add the controller to NO_PROXY, or set trust_env=False on the requests session
Switch to http:// to bypass the proxy
Set verify=False, because the CI runner's proxy re-signs the certificate and that's what causes the timeout
e: requests honors proxy environment variables, so internal calls go through a proxy that can't reach the controller. Exclude internal hosts rather than weakening TLS.

p: Several integrations call the Meraki API for one organization, and all of them see frequent 429s. Which two changes help? (Choose two.)
o: Give each integration its own API key, which brings its own rate limit
Set verify=False, which skips the TLS handshake and lowers load
Cut call volume with organization-wide endpoints and action batches
Send requests from more threads, so the queue drains faster
Honor Retry-After and back off before retrying
e: The rate limit applies per organization, whatever keys are used, so the integrations share it. Backing off and making fewer, larger calls are what reduce the 429s.

p: Which two keep device passwords out of a pyATS testbed file stored in Git? (Choose two.)
o: password written in base64, which pyATS decodes
password: "%ASK{}", which prompts at run time
password in a YAML comment, which pyATS ignores
password: "%ENV{LAB_PASS}", read from the environment
password on the same line as the device name
e: pyATS resolves %ENV{} from environment variables and %ASK{} interactively. Base64 isn't protection, and the file would still contain the secret.

p: After a port change, a script must confirm through the Meraki API that the switch ports are up at the expected speed and without errors. Which call fits?
o: GET /devices/{serial}/switch/ports
GET /devices/{serial}/switch/ports/statuses
GET /networks/{networkId}/switch/settings
GET /organizations/{organizationId}/devices/statuses
e: ports/statuses returns live state such as status, speed, duplex, errors and traffic. ports returns configuration only, and device statuses show only whether the switch is online.

p: An engineer wants to use a local terminal and scripts against the consoles of CML lab nodes, without adding an external connector. Which CML feature provides this?
o: The node's Day-0 configuration
The unmanaged switch node
Link conditioning on each node's links
The Breakout Tool, which maps node consoles to local ports
e: The Breakout Tool runs on the user's machine and forwards each node's console to a local port, so ordinary clients and scripts can use it.

p: A test must show that OSPF reconverges when a core link fails. How can this be done in a CML lab?
o: Stop the link between the two core nodes through the API, then verify the routing tables
Delete one core node and rebuild the lab after the test
Add link conditioning to the core link with very high latency, which makes OSPF treat the link as failed
Change the OSPF cost in the production network and watch the lab
e: Lab links can be stopped and started programmatically, which simulates a failure cleanly and repeatably. Latency isn't a failure, and deleting nodes loses the lab state.

p: Which request lists the images currently tagged golden in Catalyst Center?
o: GET /dna/intent/api/v1/image/importation?isTaggedGolden=true
GET /dna/intent/api/v1/image/distribution?status=golden
GET /dna/intent/api/v1/image/importation/golden
GET /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device?golden=true
e: The image list takes filters such as isTaggedGolden, family and version. The golden endpoint is used to tag or untag an image, not to list images.

p: Meraki switches across several networks must be upgraded in groups, with a delay between groups. Which API feature fits?
o: A single firmware upgrade per network, scheduled at the same time for every network
Rebooting switches in turn with POST /devices/{serial}/reboot
Staged firmware upgrades, with switch groups and a start time for each stage
Copying the image to each switch with the liveTools API
e: Staged upgrades divide MS switches into groups and schedule each stage, which limits the impact if something goes wrong. Meraki firmware isn't copied to devices by the user.

p: A request to /dna/intent/api/v1/network-health needs a timestamp. Which format does Catalyst Center expect?
o: A relative time, such as -1h
An ISO 8601 string, such as 2026-10-29T01:00:00Z
Epoch time in seconds, such as 1761700000
Epoch time in milliseconds, such as 1761700000000
e: Catalyst Center health APIs use epoch milliseconds. A value in seconds is read as a date in 1970.

p: Which Meraki call shows how many wireless clients failed at the association, authentication, DHCP and DNS steps?
o: GET /networks/{networkId}/wireless/connectionStats
GET /networks/{networkId}/clients
GET /organizations/{organizationId}/devices/statuses
GET /networks/{networkId}/wireless/clientCountHistory
e: connectionStats breaks connection attempts down by the stage where they fail. clientCountHistory only counts clients, and the clients list has no failure details.

p: Which statement about telemetry subscriptions on IOS XE is accurate?
o: The CLI can create dynamic subscriptions with telemetry ietf subscription dynamic
Dynamic subscriptions are created only with NETCONF establish-subscription; RESTCONF can only configure configured subscriptions
Configured subscriptions can only be created from the CLI, because NETCONF and RESTCONF can't change the telemetry configuration on IOS XE
RESTCONF can create dynamic subscriptions, which stream over the HTTPS connection
e: A dynamic subscription is tied to the NETCONF session that requested it. RESTCONF, NETCONF and the CLI can all edit the configuration that defines configured subscriptions.

p: Telemetry must be encrypted on the way to the collector. Which receiver setting does that?
o: receiver ip address 10.9.0.50 57500 protocol grpc-tcp encrypt
receiver ip address 10.9.0.50 57500 protocol grpc-tcp profile COLLECTOR-TP
receiver ip address 10.9.0.50 443 protocol https
receiver ip address 10.9.0.50 57500 protocol grpc-tls profile COLLECTOR-TP
e: grpc-tls encrypts the dial-out session and uses a trustpoint (profile) to validate the collector's certificate. grpc-tcp is plain text, and a VRF doesn't encrypt anything.
c:
telemetry ietf subscription 510
 encoding encode-kvgpb
 filter xpath /process-cpu-ios-xe-oper:cpu-usage/cpu-utilization
 stream yang-push
 update-policy periodic 3000
 ________

p: Which line completes this Meraki webhook receiver's check?
o: body.get("organizationId") == ORG_ID
hmac.compare_digest(body.get("sharedSecret", ""), SECRET)
hmac.compare_digest(request.headers.get("X-Cisco-Meraki-API-Key", ""), API_KEY)
body.get("sharedSecret") is SECRET
e: Meraki puts the configured shared secret in the payload's sharedSecret field. compare_digest compares it in constant time, while is tests object identity, not equality. Org IDs aren't secret, and API keys aren't sent in webhooks.

p: How does SD-WAN Manager send alarms to an external HTTPS receiver?
o: Through an alarm notification rule with a webhook URL, sent when matching alarms are raised
Through a Catalyst Center event subscription
Through a NETCONF subscription from the receiver to SD-WAN Manager
Through a device template that points each edge at the receiver
e: Alarm notifications match alarm types and severities, and send them by email or webhook. Edges don't post alarms to receivers themselves.

p: What does a peer comparison, or comparative insight, in Catalyst Center AI analytics show?
o: How a site's or device's KPIs compare with similar sites or devices, so outliers stand out
How the network compares with Cisco's lab benchmarks for each model
A comparison of two software images before an upgrade
A comparison of the running configuration with its golden template
e: Comparing like with like shows where one site or device performs worse than its peers, which a single absolute threshold can miss.

p: What's the main value of AI root-cause analysis in a controller during an outage?
o: It replaces the event logs, which aren't kept once AI analysis is on
It guarantees that the cause it finds is correct, so engineers can act on it without checking the evidence
It correlates related events across devices and suggests the likely cause, cutting through alarm noise
It fixes the cause automatically on every device
e: One failure often triggers many alarms. Correlation groups them and points to a probable cause, which engineers then confirm.

p: An AI assistant keeps producing RESTCONF payloads with wrong node names for a device. Which input most improves its accuracy?
o: The pyang tree, or the YANG modules themselves, for the exact revisions on the device
A longer instruction asking it to be careful with node names
Example payloads written for a different vendor's YANG models, so it can learn the general JSON structure
The device's hostname and serial number
e: Giving the model the real schema grounds it in the actual names and structure, instead of whatever its training data suggests.

p: An AI assistant wrote a playbook using a module that ansible-doc can't find. What's the best response?
o: Install collections from Ansible Galaxy one at a time until ansible-doc finds a module with that name
Ask the assistant to confirm that the module exists
Rename an existing module to match the assistant's name
Check the collection's documentation for the installed version and use the module it lists
e: Assistants sometimes invent modules or use deprecated ones. The installed collection's documentation, along with ansible-doc and ansible-lint, is the authority.

p: An AI agent's tools use one service account with full Catalyst Center rights for every user who chats with it. What's the main risk?
o: Responses will be less accurate for users with fewer rights
Any user can get the agent to act with rights they don't have themselves
The agent will be slower, because one account handles every call
Catalyst Center will refuse calls from service accounts
e: This is a confused-deputy problem. Each action should be checked against the requesting user's permissions, or run with credentials scoped to that user.

p: An agent builds shell commands from model output, such as ping targets, and runs them on an automation server. Which two controls reduce the risk? (Choose two.)
o: Add an instruction to the system prompt asking the model never to include shell metacharacters in values
Validate each value, for example checking that host is an IP address, before using it
Call programs with argument lists, such as subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "3", host]), never through a shell
Log nothing, so injected commands can't be traced
Run the commands as root, so they never fail on permissions
e: Without a shell, characters such as ; and | aren't interpreted. Strict validation stops unexpected values. Instructions to the model help but don't enforce anything.

p: A FastMCP tool returns a site's entire syslog history, often over 50 MB, and the agent fails or loses context. What's the best fix?
o: Return the log as a resource instead of a tool result, because resources aren't limited by the context window
Split the log over several identical tools
Add parameters such as a time range, severity and limit, and return a filtered, bounded result
Compress the result with gzip before returning it
e: Tool results go into the model's context, which is limited. Let the model ask for what it needs, and cap the size.

p: An agent keeps choosing get_device when it should call get_devices. Which two changes help it pick correctly? (Choose two.)
o: Merge them into one general tool called run, which takes any command and decides for itself what to return
Shorten both names to single letters
Write docstrings that say what each tool returns and when to use it
Give each tool a distinct name that states its scope, such as get_device_by_serial
Remove the docstrings so the model isn't distracted
e: Models choose tools from their names, descriptions and schemas. Clear, specific names and descriptions are the main levers.

p: What does the Literal type hint do for the AI client?
o: It converts any value the model sends into enabled
It becomes an enum in the input schema, so only enabled or disabled are valid
It makes state optional, with enabled as the default
It's only a hint for code editors and doesn't appear in the schema
e: FastMCP turns type hints into JSON Schema, so Literal values become an enum and other values are rejected before the function runs.
